title: Sid Catlett and Buddy Rich the greatest soloist
summary: Leeman introduces Catlett as a king of the drum throne, calls Buddy Rich the greatest soloist, and tells the story of Rich's reply to the Queen of England.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: George also was with a large band featuring Red's first wife, Mildred Bailey. More battles of music in New England. I've saved Sidney Catlett until now, a prince among fellows. But a king on the drummer's throne - that was what we called and still do, a folding drum seat. A drum throne. Sidney, considered by many drummers, historians and critics, as the greatest jazz drummer. He was very close to being that. I always had reservations about calling anyone the 'greatest' anything. Because each individual has some wonderful attributes that another great doesn't have. Thank God everybody can do a little something different than somebody else can. An exception to the rule for me is the fact that Buddy Rich is the greatest drum soloist of all time -- to me. No holds barred, and I don't believe he will ever be capped. He's one of a kind, period, and I call him a close friend.

We were playing a Command Performance for the Queen of England, and at the reception afterward, the Queen of England came up and said, "Mr. Rich, that was a wonderful performance -- how do you do it?" And Buddy, whose ego is not lacking, as we all know, at a loss for words, replied, "Just lucky I guess!"
